theme: Great businesses & AI maths · 좋은 기업과 AI 수학

tracks.title: Bill Ackman on great businesses & concentrated investing (14 min)
tracks.note: NBIM 국부펀드 CEO Nicolai Tangen이 묻고 Bill Ackman이 거의 혼자 말해요(약 13분). '좋은 회사란?' → 왜 12–14개 종목에만 집중하는지 → 정보원(WSJ, FT, Economist, X) → 레스토랑 프랜차이즈 → 투자 원칙 체크리스트 → 팀 운영 방식 순서예요. 스크립트는 자동 음성인식(whisper)이라 이름·단어가 틀린 곳이 있어요(예: 'Chris Hahn/Horn' = Chris Hohn, 'mode' = moat). 1회차는 흐름만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: Thanks for having me.

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: What's a good company?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Good or great?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Great.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: A great company is a business you could buy today.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: The markets could shut for 20 years, and you know with an enormous degree of certainty that you'll own something that's enormously valuable down to 20 years from now.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And what kind of industries are they in these great companies?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You know, I think it's less industry-specific than the structure of the business.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: They're amazing businesses in many different sectors.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And so what kind of structure does it need?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We love businesses that look like royalty-collecting companies, like annuities, where you can be very confident that the annuity will grow at a high rate over a very long period of time.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And the cash that's generated from the business doesn't need to be reinvested in the business.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Actually, Pershing Square, I'll give you the pitch.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We'll talk about that a bit better.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: How many of those companies are there in the world, you think?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: The answer is, there aren't a large number of big ones.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So from the perspective of Pershing Square, we're allocating, not the kind of capital

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: you allocate, but we're adding pretty big checks.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: That's why we're concentrating, because one, there's a limited number.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: There's probably actually a couple hundred to 300 really great businesses.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: But it's not so often that a really great business becomes available at a price that makes it a great investment.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So that's why we're concentrating.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: How do you come up with the idea?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So where do you find these things?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You know, just, you know, we love investing, we love learning about businesses, we read the newspaper, so to speak, but we sort of built a library of companies we admire.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And you know, business that has great economic characteristic, high rates of growth, managed by good management teams, they don't often become available at prices that offer the kind of returns we're looking for.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Why don't more people do like you do?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Because I think it's just interesting, you

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: know, Chris Horn has the same philosophy, Warren Buffett, and you talk about how you do it, and yet so very few people manage it.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So part of it is structural.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Well, many investors want to get rich quick.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And this is not sort of a get rich quick strategy.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You have to have kind of a longer term view.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And then I think most of the capital in the asset management industry is inherently short term, available for redemption on a minute by minute, day by day, or quarterly, or annual basis.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: basis, it's hard to think long-term if your investors are going to be judging on a very short-term basis, or the person you work for.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Think the citadels, the millenniums, firms where very short-term oriented use a high degree of financial leverage.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You can't absorb a high degree of volatility in a strategy like that, whereas the Warren Buffett's had permanent capital, Chris Hahn has been in the business for a long period of time.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: He's cultivated investors that have given him long-term backing.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You need that in order to implement the strategy and that kind of capital is very scarce.

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: Tell me a bit more where you

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: get your information from.

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: What do you read?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Personally, I read Wall Street Journal, FT, Economist, occasionally the New York Times when I can stomach it.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: No, it's a good newspaper.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: All media have biases.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I spend a fair amount of time on X, actually.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It's probably my most important source of information because you can follow people who have very much diverging views on the same topic, and I think it's a very good way to get to the truth.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: That's become increasingly a big source of where I get my media.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Who do you follow?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I follow probably 1,000 people over time.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It depends on the topic.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I've got lots of different interests, and interestingly, some of the firm's best investments and some of my personal best ideas have just come from particular passions.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Health being an important passion led me to an insight about COVID.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I started seeing COVID emerge in January, got concerned about a pandemic.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And my interest was not driven by an investment perspective, but it led to an interesting investment opportunity.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Now a family tragedy is causing me to

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: spend a lot of time learning about what's going on AI and bringing computer interfaces.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: is, and it may lead to some interesting investment opportunities.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So once we find something that's interesting, due diligence is driven by fairly conventional looking at public filings and then talking to, using expert networks to talk to people.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We'll come back to your

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: tragedy.

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: How much time do you spend on X?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: My wife might say too much.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: What is that?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I don't I don't calculate it.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: What do you think?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: What do you think an hour a day or more?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I would say It's usually in the morning in the evening and not during the the business day, but it depends on what else is going on my life, but I can spend It's a it's actually interesting thing is People who are on X versus people who rely on conventional media You've generally feel like you're a week to two weeks ahead like news comes out and you learn that a week ago So it's very much a real-time source of information.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You made a lot of money in restaurants.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Why have they been good investments?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Simple, predictable, free cash flow, generative businesses.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We've kind of focused on, for the most part, kind of the franchise business model.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Again, royalty collecting companies.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: But it's, I think, over time you build a domain expertise in an area.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It's just that my daughter runs a cocktail bar and it's not an easy business, huh?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It's not.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It's not but again.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It's it's less the sector than the structure hmm You know McDonald's is an amazing business, but it's really people think of it as a historically thought of it as a restaurant business But I mean in its core it is but it's also a real estate business,

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: and it's a franchising operation how much do Do you depend on

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: your?

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: Your pattern recognition or your gut feel the fact that you've seen these things play out before I

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I don't know if, I think it's very valuable to have experienced lots of market events over time.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You know, we've kind of, I think it's, but importantly for us, actually, you see that little tablet over there, we took our current core investment principles and we created what amounts to a checklist.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We have a framework.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And so I think that's, I would say, that framework that helps us see the world in a way, which every once in a

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: while surfaces an interesting investment opportunity.

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: So, we'll now look at this thing here and we'll zoom in on it afterwards, but just what are the most important things there?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: One, it's a business we can predict with a very high degree of confidence, right?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: The value of a financial asset is the present value that cash will generate over its life.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: If you can't build a model of the next, you know, reasonable period of time of a business, 10, 15, 20 years, I don't think you can come up with the value for it.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: A lot of money is managed based on people believing a stock will go up or down based on a new piece of information coming out, but it's inherently a short-term, you know, it's going to come

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: to going to meet, exceed or miss earnings.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: A huge amount of money is moved on that basis or an expectation of an event or a news event that will cause a stock to move in a certain way.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We kind of ignore that, right?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: What we're doing is we're building a financial model of a company over a long period of time.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So the business has to be inherently, there are many businesses that we have no idea what they're worth.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We just don't even look at them.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Or once we conclude they're not, we can't predict their certainty.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So I think predictability is important.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And obviously to have predictable cash flows and revenues over time, the business has to have the proverbial mode around it.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So business, quality, durability, I would say critically important.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We want companies that are not exposed to, we call extrinsic factors we can't control.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So we don't really invest in commodity sensitive businesses, interest rate sensitive businesses, as regulatory sensitive businesses.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So it's about, we keep it simple.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Well, at least your principles are set in stone, right?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Exactly, that was intended to be.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I told the guy on the team to make it stone.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We came back with a heavy plastic.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: How do you use the analysts?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So, you're like just under 50 people in the

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: firm.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I would say the firm is structured differently from Chris Hahn.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Yeah, we're 48 people.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We're nine investment professionals.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And it's not me and a team of analysts.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It's actually an investment team.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You know, Ryan Israel became our CIO, you know, four years ago.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: But a typical structure of a hedge fund is you have a portfolio manager, I guess that's normally my position, who's responsible for allocating capital among a team of analysts who are working on kind of different areas, and the best ideas win, and people are compensated based on individual P&Ls.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We're not structured that way.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: One portfolio of 12, 14 investments.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: investments, no one is compensated based on individual P&Ls.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Everyone's compensated ultimately based on how the overall portfolio does.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Their interest is not getting capital allocated to them.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Their interest is making sure our firm's capital is allocated and our investor's capital is allocated in a way that makes the most sense.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So how does it work?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So you sit around this table here?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: This is not, we have an investment team room, which is smaller than this, half the size.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So there you are, you meet every week or how do you?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: The team has a formal meeting every week, but we have lunch together almost every day at the full team.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So very high degree of interaction in the team.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Typically someone identifies an interesting idea.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It could be me, it

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: could be Ryan, it could be a member of the team.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Hey, XYZ stock, a company we filed for years is now available at 40% discount because they missed earnings.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Let's update the file.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So we plot the file, the team that has done the most work on the name, we'll dig in again, update their work, typically a two-person team, Ryan

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: and or I will effectively oversee that team by doing some amount of work.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So I'll read the end reports, the proxy, the conference call transcripts, maybe some news articles.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: The team doing the deeper dive will speak to many industry experts.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: we'll do a kind of deep dive and then the whole team work on one idea at the time two people will work on one idea and go deep two people who do have done some work that's you know Ryan and Ryan and then the rest of them will have done no work on the name and then that whole group will form a view as to whether and the team who leads the work will build a PowerPoint presentation and present to the team you know why they think an investment is is interesting and then and make a collective decision.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: But actually, an important dynamic is the typical hedge fund instruction in such a way your only incentive is to get capital allocated to deal, which sort of causes you to kind of lean in to wanting an idea to be in the portfolio.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: In our case, we'll have two people who've done the work in a very profound way, two people who have done some of the work and a group that has nothing invested in terms of time.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Do you need to have consensus?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: instances?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: If there is an objection or someone raises a concern, we do more due diligence to address the objection.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Ultimately, I have the final say, but I can't think of an investment in the last decade that we didn't have really a collective view on.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So let's take an

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: example like you on Brookfield.

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: How does that work?

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: How long time does it take from when

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: you start to look at it until you make the investment?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So, we got to know, I got to know Bruce Flatt and the senior Brookfield team working on a transaction.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So, FYI, Brookfield is the private equity Canadian group.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So, I met Bruce Flatt in connection with the bankruptcy of General Growth, where they were, we ended up partnering with them and doing a restructuring of that company, got to know the team really well, had enormous respect for, you know, came to have enormous respect for Bruce and Cyrus and other members of that team that today still run that company.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: But we never invested in Brookfield.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Then the company over time restructured and became a bit more of an asset light royalty collecting business, and then we began to do diligence process a number of years ago.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Brookfield's actually quite a complicated company.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It's one of the reasons why it's attractively valued.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: They've been simplifying the business over time.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: But it was probably a several-month due diligence process that led to that investment.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Is it more difficult to beat the market now than it was when you started?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I would say we don't try to beat the market every month or even every quarter or every year.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: But I think managing a concentrated pool of capital and having the ability to have a longer-term view, I think, gives you a big competitive advantage in terms of beating the market over the long term.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: But the market's been an amazing competitor, there, if you will, the index.

transcript.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: Now, what is AI doing to the market?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: I think it's making market participants increasingly shorter and shorter term.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You know, you can a 10K gets published, and AI can read it instantly.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: There's a huge amount of capital invested in looking for a short term, short term edge.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: And AI, I think, enables that.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: The type of investments you have, which are AI related would be, I mean, you got AWS, anything else?

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So, you know, Meta is a big investor in, well, I would say every business today is either AI related or should be, or is going to be disrupted by AI.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: So I think that's the assessment that you have to do.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: You know, we own, we purchased Amazon after Trump announced the liberation date tariffs.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: We acquired Meta after they disappointed people by committing a large amount of money to CapEx, and the same with Microsoft.

transcript.speaker: Bill Ackman
transcript.text: It's sort of an interesting environment when you have a company come out publicly and say, we have enormous demand for our service, therefore we have to invest well in excess of what we expected in CapEx just to try to meet the demand from our product and then...

listening.task: 오늘은 Bill Ackman(Pershing Square)이 노르웨이 국부펀드 NBIM의 팟캐스트 'In Good Company'(2026년 10월 28일)에서 한 인터뷰 앞부분 14분이에요. 출근길에 1배속(어려우면 0.75배속)으로 한 번 흐름만 듣고, 퇴근길에 한 번 더 들어요. 'royalty-collecting companies', 'get rich quick', 'permanent capital', 'a very high degree of confidence'가 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요. 바쁘면 Part 1의 처음 5분(좋은 회사의 정의 ~ 'get rich quick')만 들어도 OK예요.

quiz.q: Why does Pershing Square own only a small number of companies? a) Its team is too small to follow more stocks, b) There are only a few hundred truly great businesses, and they are rarely available at a great price, c) Short-term trading on earnings news is more profitable
quiz.answer: b) Ackman은 정말 훌륭한 기업이 전 세계에 200–300개 정도뿐이고, 그런 기업이 '좋은 투자'가 될 만한 가격에 나오는 일은 드물어서 집중투자한다고 해요. c)는 오히려 그가 무시한다고 말한 단기 매매 방식이에요.

reading.title: AI has conquered mathematics’ greatest challenge
reading.source: The Economist (public reprint via Hindustan Times)
reading.summaryKo: 1859년 Riemann이 제시한 '리만 가설'이 167년 만에 증명됐대요. 11월 20일 Anthropic의 수학자 Levent Alpöge가 AI 모델 Claude와 함께 증명 검증 언어 Lean으로 1,700만 줄짜리 증명을 만들었고, 독립된 두 팀이 21일에 정확하다고 확인했어요. 9월 이후 AI로 풀린 오래된 수학 난제가 수백 개에 달한다고 해요. 그런데 '증명이 맞는 건 아는데, 그 증명이 무엇인지는 모른다'(Kevin Buzzard)는 상황이라, 인간 수학자의 역할과 '이론 구축(theory building)'이 앞으로 어떻게 될지가 큰 질문이래요.
excerpt: IN 1859 BERNHARD RIEMANN, a German mathematician who had been pondering the nature of prime numbers, came up with a new mathematical entity, known as the “zeta function”. Proving Riemann right became the greatest of white whales for generations of mathematicians. This week, after a 167-year hunt, it was caught.
“Right now we’re in this ridiculous, never seen before, situation where we know the proof is correct, but we just don’t know what the proof is,” says Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London.
reading.tip: 'white whale'은 소설 Moby-Dick에서 온 표현으로 '평생 쫓는 집요한 목표'라는 뜻이에요. 기사 전체가 사냥 비유(hunt, caught, pounced)로 이어지니 같이 찾아보세요. 'lodestar'(길잡이별, 지침)도 Economist가 좋아하는 단어예요.

writing.prompt: Write 3–5 sentences in English: Ackman says a great company is one you could buy today and happily own even if the market shut for 20 years. Name one company you would own that way, and explain why.
writing.question: What makes that business predictable? Does it have a 'moat'?
writing.hint: 이런 표현을 써 보세요: I would happily own ... for 20 years because ... / Its moat is ... / I can predict its cash flow because ...

speaking.prompt: In one minute: AI just helped prove a 167-year-old maths problem. How do you use AI at work or in coding? Does this news excite you or worry you?
phrases: What worries me a little is ...
